{"id": "55042f29-1ca1-4690-86fd-91404e1b8b93", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I don't have a dedicated sustainability-reporting skill loaded in this agent space, so I can't run a specific carbon-analysis workflow for you — but I pulled the relevant facts from AWS's own documentation on the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool (CCFT), and they point to a few concrete explanations. Your optimization almost certainly didn't fail — the reported number and the actual effect are probably just out of sync.

**1. Reporting lag — likely the biggest factor**
CCFT data is published 15th–21st of the *following* month, and AWS only recently expanded the tool. If you migrated "last quarter," the emissions benefit of moving 40 TB to Deep Archive may not be fully reflected yet in what you're looking at — you could be comparing a month where the migration overhead landed against a month where the steady-state savings haven't caught up.

**2. Methodology version changes, not your workload**
AWS updated CCFT to a new v2.0 methodology (Jan 2025 onward uses v2.0, December 2024 and earlier uses v1.0), and as of October 2025 CCFT now also includes **Scope 3 emissions** (manufacturing, transport, lifecycle impact) plus Scope 1 natural gas/refrigerants that weren't counted before. If your "before" baseline predates these changes and your "after" number includes them, you're comparing two different measurement standards, not a real increase from your migration. This alone can make a well-optimized account look worse period-over-period.

**3. One-time transition overhead**
Moving objects into Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive adds 40 KB of metadata overhead *per archived object* (8 KB billed at S3 Standard rate, 32 KB at the Glacier rate). At scale across many small objects, this is a real (if small) one-time storage and processing bump that would show up as a short-term uptick around the migration event — separate from any genuine ongoing increase.

**4. Check what else changed**
Carbon reporting is account/region-wide, not per-bucket. If other workloads (compute, other storage, different regions with a different grid carbon intensity) grew in the same quarter, that growth could dominate the trend even though your S3 line item genuinely went down.

**What I'd suggest to actually confirm this:**
- Pull your CCFT numbers broken out by **AWS Region** and by service (CCFT now supports regional granularity) rather than looking at the total.
- Use **AWS Data Exports** for carbon data to get gram-level resolution and isolate the S3 line item specifically, rather than the account-wide rollup.
- Compare month-over-month using the *same* methodology version — don't mix pre-2025 and post-2025 figures.

If you want, I can look into your account's actual CCFT trend and S3 storage-class distribution to see whether the increase is isolated to S3 or coming from elsewhere.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
